appraisal_events.evidence: "C'est quelqu'un de très mal... De très, très mal"; elle dit avec une emphase ironique le nom : le Prince de Borodino, en femme pour qui l'Empire ne compte pas.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme de Villeparisis, voicing Robert's family's anger at Borodino for enabling the liaison, morally condemns him as 'very, very bad,' but the narrator's remark that this is 'l'accent vertueux des Guermantes même les plus dépravés' and her sarcastic stress on his Napoleonic title expose that the blame mixes real disapproval with aristocratic snobbery toward Empire-created nobility.

appraisal_events.evidence: "il était lui-même très mal élevé, combien ses paroles déplaisaient"; l'anecdote "resta incompréhensible pour les personnes présentes"; "cet accent d'enthousiasme qu'on n'apporte qu'aux convictions qu'on ne s'est pas formées soi-même."
appraisal_events.explanation: While Bloch praises Saint-Loup's good breeding, the narrator repeatedly exposes Bloch's own ill-bred manner, his misjudgment in treating Sir Rufus Israël as a mark of prestige (an assessment the Guermantes milieu does not share), and his borrowed, unoriginal enthusiasm, locally diminishing him before the gathered company.

status_effects.explanation: Borodino is branded 'très, très mal' and 'l'horrible capitaine,' accused of favoring an infamous liaison, sharply lowering his local standing.

Villeparisis's ironic emphasis on the title 'le Prince de Borodino' signals that, for old-nobility Guermantes, his Napoleonic-created rank does not count as real nobility, locally discounting his social standing.
Bloch's tactless manner, his failed anecdote, and his imitative enthusiasm are narrated as unflattering exposures of his social gaucherie.
His anecdote, meant as persuasive proof of Saint-Loup's breeding, lands flat and incomprehensible for his aristocratic audience, undercutting his rhetorical authority.
Contrary to Bloch's near-royal estimation of him, the narrator states the Guermantes milieu regards Rufus Israël as a merely tolerated parvenu foreigner whose friendship confers no prestige.

ambiguities: The blame of Borodino originates both in 'la famille de Robert' generally and in Mme de Villeparisis's own speech to the narrator; the two are treated as aligned but the passage does not fully distinguish family sentiment from her personal judgment.

Bloch's praise of Saint-Loup's good breeding appears genuine, but the anecdote meant to prove it falls flat with the aristocratic audience due to a clash in social values, leaving unclear whether it registers as any elevation for Saint-Loup or is entirely absorbed into Bloch's own exposure.
